This document presents usual steps to **convert a R script** to a **Quarto** (Qmd) document.

<br>
<br>

## Training preparation

Create and open a Rstudio Server Core session.

From it :

- Go to your project
- Create a new `Initiation_Quarto` directory
- Enter it

```{r}
#| label: setwd
#| filename: setwd

project_name <- "ebaii_sc_teachers"

if (dir.exists(paths = paste0("/shared/projects/", project_name))) {
  
  iq_dir <- paste0("/shared/projects/", project_name, "/Initiation_Quarto")
  dir.create(path = iq_dir, recursive = TRUE)
  setwd(iq_dir)

} else message("Project name [", project_name, "] not found !!")

```

Then :

- Synch your `Files` browser *(grey arrow)*
- Upload *(button that represents a sheet with an orange disc, with an "up" white arrow)* :
  - `basic_analysis.R`
  - `sobj.rds`

Now you're fine to start.

We'll pretend you just finished an analysis contained in the `basic_analysis.R` script.

## Open your R script

It may contain :

- calls to libraries (`library()`)
- comments (`## blah blah`)
- codelines to :
  - load data
  - transform data
  - plot
  - *etc ...*

## Create a brand new Quarto script

... using `File` > `New File` > `R Quarto document`

You can name it **whatever you want** *(as long as its extension remains `.Qmd`)*

::: {.callout-note}
Two options :

- Create an **empty document** to start from scratch, save it as `Qmd`
- Use a Quarto **template**, customize and save it.
  - This is what happens when creating a Quarto document form the Rstudio menu
  - This is the most practical way
  - One can create and use its own template(s)
  - This is how the current document was created !
:::

A Quarto document is structured with :

- A **header** : many options are possible to customize style

- Code **chunks** to write with **programming language**

- **Empty space** between chunks to write in **natural language**

::: {.callout-note}
To insert a code chunk in Rstudio (Server), you can use :

- The **menu** : `Code` > `Insert chunk`
- A keyboard **shortcut** :
  - For Linux/Win : `<CTRL>` + `<ALT>` + `<I>`
  - For Mac : `<OPTION>` + `<COMMAND>` + `<I>`

It should create something like that in your Qmd :

```{{r}}

```

:::

## First layer : basics

### Filling

The easiest way to start is to :

- **Create a chunk** in your newly created Qmd document
- Copy-paste **all** of your R script content inside
- **Render** it : `::> Knit`
- Wait for the magic to happen !

::: {.callout-note}
In the end, a new file named as your `.Qmd` script but with a `.html` extension has been created (along the Quarto script)
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
If a `.html` file with the same name already existed, **it would be overwritten without warning** !!
:::

### Observations

This way, you :

- Added a pinch of **traceability** :
  - You generated a first **static** output (the `.html`) that you won't edit.
- Have your code, comments and outputs **alltogether** ! These outputs include :
  - Functions textual output (messages, warnings, ...)
  - Plots
- One single output file that can be easily **shared**


## Second layer : slicing

### Code splitting

You can now **split** your unique chunk in multiple, smaller, well delimited and structured chunks 

To do so, you can either :

- Create iteratively new chunks after the main one, cut & paste the parts you want to extract.
- Position the cursor where you would like to split your main chunk and use the `<CTRL>` + `<ALT>` + `<I>` (or `<OPTION>` + `<COMMAND>` + `<I>` if you like apples).
  - It is the easiest way, according to me :)

### Free text extraction

Once all smaller chunks are created, one can **extract free text** (comments, conclusions, etc ...) from the chunks to "inter-chunks" regions.

Then, knit !

### Observations

This time you added a pinch of **structure** to your document :

- Spliting the unique blob of chunk to specific commands/blocs
- Separating code and free text in different sections

## Third layer : beautification

### Chunks

(Technical) comments can be added in chunks when needed.

Chunks can be shaped with many, many [parameters](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html). These control :

- Their appearance in the output document
- Their inclusion in the output document
- Same for their console output (text, plot)
- etc ...

::: {.callout-note}
It is recommended to **name** your chunks. It way easier for debugging when knitting : the rendering engine (knitr/pandoc) tells the chunk name that contains an error.

Here is an example where the chunk is named (`#| label: `), and a trick to make this name appear in the HTML output (`#| filename: `).

```{{r}}
#| label: my_chunk_is_named
#| filename: my_chunk_is_named

## Where am I on the cluster instance ?
getwd()
```
:::

### Free text

It can be shaped, finely structured. It can be formatted in the [**markdown**](https://www.markdownguide.org/basic-syntax/) syntax.

By example :

- add titles using `#` (first level), subtitles using `##` (second level) etc ..., up to 6 !
- format the text
  - italic : \**italic text*\* or (\__italic text_\_)
  - bold : \*\***bold text**\*\*
  - and [much more](https://www.markdownguide.org/cheat-sheet/) !
- one can create panels, columns ...

## Forth layer : good practice

Our document is rich, beautiful to read.
Now, we may add stuff that can be useful to others (our future-self included)

In order of appearance :

- Header :
  - A **meaningful title**
  - The **author** name(s) and mail contact
  - The **current date** : ie, the *knitting* date, to remember when the analysis + rendering was done

- Free text :
  - **Explained purpose** of the document
  - Add **links** to resources of interest (papers, documentation)

- Special chunks, each dedicated to :
  - Citing the location of the `R` library(ies) used, thanks the `**.libPaths()**` function
  - Loading libraries (I recommend using explicit call to functions with `packagename::function()`)
  - Setting **global parameters**
    - paths
    - RNG seed
    - variables that have an impact throughout the analysis
    - etc ...
  - **Sourcing** outside code (code stored in other R scripts)
  - Loading **input data**
  - Citing the **packages** that were loaded throughout the analysis with `utils::sessionInfo()` (usually at the very end of the document)

## In practice

In practice, when a report is needed or an added value, we usually start with a Quarto **template**, add/fill header, code chunks, comments and formatting **while progressing** in the analysis, rather than post-processing a script.

::: {.callout-important}
Applying programming best pratices should never be done while working, nor at the end, but from scratch...
:::
